newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo seen forgiving most inter-company debt.
newsitem.headline: Yugo seen forgiving most inter-company debt.

text.p: Yugoslavia's central bank has introduced a compulsory inter-company debt settlement scheme to ease the swollen internal debt, but analysts said on Thursday the whole operation will eventually lead to a debt write-off.

The central bank's Accounting and Payments Operations Office (ZOP) has begun the first round of a highly technical debt-settlement scheme, to be performed in six monthly cycles and for the first time obliging the state to report its liabilities to budget recepients.

"The need for compulsory multilateral compensation arose due to the extremely high level of matured short-term debt which stood at 101 billion dinars ($17.1 billion) at the end of 1996," Zivko Nesic, ZOP general manager told a news conference.
The amount, accumulated over last several years, was seen exceeding Yugoslavia's GDP by 50 percent on an annual basis.
Financial analysts feared the multilateral compensation would not do the job as some of the biggest debtors were state firms which they say would remain protected.

"The state always has a pet company which remains privileged on the good political backing of its manager. Such a firm will not have to report its debt or enter the scheme," said an analyst who spoke under condition of anonymity.
Debt incurred by state favourites could be compensated from the state budget or central bank credits, but economists cast doubt the heavily indebted state could afford to assume new liabilities.
"Eventually the debt will be written-off. They have no financial capacity to service it and the easiest way is to annul it," an economist said.
All firms and the state must report their matured debt by July 31. Debts will be "cleared" in the last week of the month.

In practice, ZOP will be a match-maker, creating circles of debtors involving as many participants as possible and trying to clear the debt by pouring into the chain the lowest possible amount to clear the debt.
The accounts of 25,000 firms employing around 900,000 people were either permanently or occasionally blocked and their outstanding debt has reached 8.8 billion dinars in 1997.

The government engineered scheme will be divided into two stages, the first of which will involve simple debt reporting and "clearing" in cases where both the debtor and the creditor are known and ready to finalise the deal.

For the second stage, the government advised commercial banks to open up their credit portfolio to "reliable" clients, at the same time promising the state would not tap the central bank for any funds to compensate the ballooning debt.
Both stages will be performed during each monthly cycle.
The multilateral compensation is hoped to improve financial discipline and increase liquidity of companies and banks. -- Belgrade newsroom +381 11 311 4254
